articles.title: Everett Link Draft EIS Review
articles.author: Wesley Lin
paras: On September 18, Sound Transit released the Environmental impact Statement for the Everett Link extension . This light rail extension will extend the Link light rail system north towards Everett from Lynnwood. The first phase plans to build the West Alderwood , Ash Way , Mariner , and finally the SW Everett Industrial Center by 2037. The second phase would extend it north to Everett with SR 526/Evergreen and Everett Station by 2041. There is also one unfunded provisional station at SR 99/Airport Road .
The draft EIS comment period is open until November 2nd.

This article will mostly focus on the first phase up to SW Everett Industrial Center. Most of the station alignments were previously discussed in The Urbanist as well. This discussion will focus on the details of the preferred options. Unless otherwise cited, all images are from the Sound Transit online open house .
From Lynnwood station, the line would continue north along the west side of I-5 then turn east near 33rd Ave W.

Among the alternatives considered, the preferred alternative is ALD-2D (Northern Mall Alignment with 33rd Avenue Station) shown in green. The first stop is West Alderwood next to Alderwood Mall. High retail activity and surrounding apartments should drive strong ridership.
The ALD-2D option will place the elevated station to the west of Alderwood Mall next to the JC Penney.
For the preferred alternative of ALD-D the three bus routes of 121, 122, and Swift orange would stop there. For the other alternatives of ALD-B and ALD-F the Swift Orange bus might skip the station.

There are some alternative options moving the station to the north or south of Alderwood Mall instead. Most of them have moderate tradeoffs with which properties would need to displaced. All of them would cost approximately the same at $1 billion.

From Alderwood Mall, the line would the continue north along I-5. There is no preferred alternative for this segment. The Ash Way station would be near the 164th St SW and I-5 intersection. The Swift Orange BRT would help connect residents along 164th St SW to the station. The line would reuse the existing Ash Way Park-and-Ride for parking.
ASH-1A (West of I-5 Alignment with Ash Way Park-and-Ride Station) has the line staying west of I-5. This would build the elevated Ash Way station next to the Ash Way Park-and-Ride.

The other option ASH-2D (East of I-5 Alignment with 164th Street Station) would build it on the east of I-5. One complication is that this would be complicated for the station to connect to the existing west transit facilities.
Snohomish County explored fixing the east station issues with the I-5/164th St SW Direct Access Improvements project to build an HOV/pedestrian bridge just north of 164th Street.
Assuming the I-5 overpass is built, the routes 112, 121, m103, 117, n14 and m2 will terminate at Ash Way. Swift Orange line will also using the crossing and continue along it.

The option ASH-1A staying on the west of I-5 supposedly costs more than ASH-2D. However, I’m somewhat skeptical of the numbers considering ASH-2D requires an expensive bridge across I-5 while ASH-1A stays on the same side.
After Ash Way, the line will continue north along I-5 to the Mariner Station. Clusters of garden-style apartments along 128th St SW will generate strong residential ridership.
The MAR-1B (South of 128th Street Alignment with 8th Avenue Station) alternative will build the elevated Mariner station just south of 128th St SW.
The Mariner station would serve as the transfer point for many bus routes around South Everett.
The Swift Orange will likely be extended one mile and terminate at Mariner Station instead of its current terminus at McCollum P&R.

Once the line reaches Mariner, the train will then head west along Airport Road. There is the provisional unfunded SR 99 / Airport Road station at the intersection. This SR 99 / Airport Road is surrounded by mostly light industrial and commercial properties however it would also be a pretty vital half-way point transfer point for the Swift Blue BRT line.

The SW Everett Industrial Center station (a somewhat laborious way to say Boeing) will be built near Paine Field and the Everett Boeing factory. There has been some competing priorities of whether to build this station on the north nearby Boeing for the workers or whether to build it to the west near Paine Field for passengers.
The SWI-1A (Airport Road/SR 526 Alignment with SR 526 Station) is the preferred Alternative. This would place it closest to the Seaway Transit center that Boeing workers currently use.
One complication is that most of the buses would have to take a circuitous route to reach the Seaway Transit Center. A pedestrian bridge might be built to connect the station to Boeing across SR 526.

The SWI-1B alternative places it in the mid point between the airport and Boeing. While the SWI-1C alternative places the station closest to the airport. Also interestingly, there would be an airport shuttle bus with all three station sites from the station to Paine Field airport.
These next two stations will be built in a later phase by 2041.
After SW Everett Industrial Center, the line will continue east along SR 526 to SR 526/Evergreen station. There are five alternatives here with much community pushback. We’ll go over EGN-A and EGN-E.

The EGN-A alternative will place it just north of the SR 526 freeway with the least property impacts. This places it closer to apartments such as the Four Corners and the Cascade High School. A pedestrian bridge will be built to make it easier to cross south of the freeway. However, it is also tricky to transfer to some buses.
The EGN-E places it just south of W Casino Road.
Both alternatives would connect to the Swift Blue and the future Swift Silver Line (labeled as a rerouted Green Line above).
One advantage of the EGN-E station closer to Casino Ave, is that it is easier for a bus to reach Everett Mall.
The main preferred alternative is EVT-1A (Smith Avenue Alignment) which places the Everett light rail station closest to the existing Sounder Everett station.
EVT-A would be an elevated station at the corner of Smith Ave and 32nd St.

Sound Transit has not yet decided where to place the new Operations and Maintenance Facility (OMF). One of the above three spots will be picked. The OMF is used for train maintenance, cleaning, and storage.

The projected ridership with the initial phase (in green) and second phase (in pink) is shown above. The highest daily ridership is projected at Everett Station with 10,700 riders. The next two highest are Ash Way and Mariner with approximately 4,600 riders. Mariner would have an estimated 7,000 riders (2,400 more) with the initial phase due to I-5 freeway buses from Everett truncating there.

The Everett Link extension will mostly benefit trips within the Everett and North Lynnwood area and not improve the freeway trips between Everett and destinations south of Lynnwood. Sound Transit estimates 29 minutes from Lynnwood station to Everett station which is on par with the current freeway bus times.

The original operating plan for the ST3 calls for the 3 Line to serve all stations between Lynnwood and Everett. In addition, the 2 Line will be extended to Mariner station. During peak hours, Sound Transit plans to provide 3 minute frequency for the West Alderwood, Ash Way, and Mariner stations. North of Mariner, frequency will drop to 6 minutes.

With the phased implementation plan, the exact operation plan is not clear. In addition, the exact lines that serve the new stations will also depend on the opening timelines for other ST3 extensions to West Seattle and Ballard.

articles.title: Seattle-based sales tech company Outreach to move HQ to Adobe’s campus in Fremont neighborhood
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Outreach confirmed plans to move its headquarters from Interbay to Seattle’s Fremont neighborhood early next year, joining a campus that Adobe has anchored since the late 1990s.
The sales technology company, which was valued at more than $4.4 billion in a 2021 funding round, has grown to about 800 employees from 680 in late 2024.

The company will take one floor at Fremont Lake Union Center , a three-building, roughly 424,000-square-foot campus on North 34th Street owned by Kilroy Realty. Outreach’s new space is at 701 N. 34th St., a four-story building next door to Adobe’s longtime Seattle office.

Outreach CEO Abhijit Mitra disclosed the move to the Puget Sound Business Journal , saying it would bring more face-to-face collaboration. Outreach confirmed the plans to GeekWire. The company is currently based at 333 Elliott in Interbay, where it leased the top three floors of the Martin Selig Real Estate building in 2018. It has since cut back to two floors, the PSBJ reports.
The move will bring Outreach back to Fremont. Before 333 Elliott, the company occupied about 26,000 square feet in the neighborhood, subleased from Tableau, GeekWire reported at the time.

Adobe, which established its Seattle presence by acquiring PageMaker maker Aldus in 1994, moved to the Fremont campus from Pioneer Square in 1998, becoming the anchor tenant of what was then called Quadrant Lake Union Center.

Adobe renewed and extended its lease on 163,000 square feet in 2018. The campus has seen other changes more recently: Salesforce-owned Tableau left the 837 N. 34th St. building in 2024, and co-working company Kiln is preparing to open its first Washington location in the building, with doors set to open late this year.
Tableau remains in the neighborhood. The Salesforce unit renewed its lease in July on roughly 114,000 square feet at its Data 1 building, 744 N. 34th St.
Google plans to eventually leave its longtime Fremont offices and is in the process of consolidating its Seattle employees in South Lake Union, GeekWire reported last year.

Founded in 2014, Outreach makes AI tools that research prospects, take notes during sales meetings, coach reps in real time and update CRM systems. Its customers include Zoom, Siemens and Snowflake. Co-founder Manny Medina stepped down as CEO in 2024, and Mitra, who joined in 2023 as president of product and technology, took over.

articles.title: Mapping the buffer: Inside the safety and design planning for Broadway’s Crisis Center
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: As renovations begin on the former Polyclinic building that spans between Broadway and Harvard along Union, local safety planning for King County’s upcoming Central Crisis Care Center is moving forward on two tracks: an immediate evaluation of neighborhood security gaps and an eventual handoff to an operator-run advisory council once patients arrive.

Last week , CHS reported on the political process across two mayoral administrations that formed a new six-member advisory group responsible for a crucial $3 million safety and community plan to help the surrounding neighborhoods make a better home for the new crisis center when it opens in 2027.
Here is a look at what the group has been working on, the challenges and shortcomings it is facing — and a critical handoff that must be executed with a new group once the center opens.

CHS reported here on the 2025 approval of the $56 million plan to acquire the property, overhaul the building, and hire an operator for what is planned to be the second in a network of five county facilities providing 24-7 walk-in and emergency care mental health clinics funded by a 2023 voter-approved levy.

In November , CHS reported on the selection of Connections Health Solutions to operate the center designed to provide 24/7 walk-in care, 23-Hour Observation Units for patients brought in by police “to receive immediate care to stabilize and stay for up to 23 hours,” and “crisis stabilization beds” where individuals can stay for up to 14 days “to receive focused behavioral health treatment.”

The Broadway center’s budget includes $15 million for the costs of upgrading the facility and funding the contract operator. The facility is under renovation with an expected opening by late 2027, serving as an alternative to jail or emergency rooms for adults across Seattle’s First Hill and Capitol Hill neighborhoods.

At its Kirkland center, Connections says insurance coverage for patients included approximately 50% to 60% on Medicaid, around 10% Commercial, and the rest uninsured with the levy and county contracts bridging the remaining funding. Under that deal, Connections was funded to purchase the $39 million Kirkland facility and operate the 24/7 mental health care center. Connections says more than 70% of individuals served in 2025 in Kirkland were stabilized and discharged with follow-up care plans.

Ahead of the Broadway opening, the pre-launch Seattle Community Advisory Group (SCAG) has focused heavily on surrounding street conditions. During an April session, members raised worries over “open-air drug markets, gun violence, property crime, and disorder,” warning that without strong post-crisis discharge planning, “people across King County could concentrate issues in Capitol and First Hill”.

To evaluate the physical property, King County hired an outside consultant in April to run a Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) study. Initial walk-throughs will produce design recommendations for project architect Stantec to evaluate and price out ahead of an October deadline.

DCHS noted that while SPD, the King County Sheriff’s Office, and the Mayor’s Office are contributing input, an independent consultant was hired to maintain “neutrality”—a decision that raised some frustrations among meeting participants who favored direct coordination with SPD on security planning.

Outside the former Polyclinic facility, the county’s Emergency Service Patrol , already providing “transportation, sobering, and intensive case management services to homeless chronic substance abusers” in the area, launched increased neighborhood rounds in May, covering a “1/4 mile radius around the facility” at “twice per shift.”

In July, DCHS held an open house and resource fair at 1145 Broadway, attended by SCAG members. According to a county report on the event, more than 170 neighbors, providers, and civic leaders attended. Jennifer Winslow , strategic manager for the crisis center levy, detailed upgrades underway at the former Polyclinic building, including lighting improvements, landscaping, daily trash cleanups, and baseline site security. Joel Conger of Connections Health Solutions outlined plans for walk-in urgent care, 23-hour observation, first-responder drop-offs, and youth services, estimating that building renovations will start in late 2026 toward an opening in “December 2027, at the earliest.”
Building plans also detail 16 voluntary residential treatment beds for 30-to-60-day stays, while architects review whether an adjacent triangular parcel can serve as outdoor space for clients.

Accountability tools have been another major point of discussion for the advisory group. Board members argued that an upcoming Good Neighbor Agreement must function as a “binding commitment with quantitative performance metrics, reporting requirements, and adaptive management responses”. County officials explained that Connections is drafting the document to outline shared obligations between the provider, city, and county, with public feedback scheduled for 2027.

To guide its December funding vote on a $3 million county mitigation pool, the group has established a half-mile radius around 1145 Broadway to map service gaps, covering the area from Seattle Central College to Seattle University . The board is reviewing existing private security patrols run by local hospitals and colleges, and waiting on a Seattle City Council study of nearby supportive housing and human services, to ensure the funding fills actual holes rather than duplicating existing work.
While SCAG handles pre-opening planning and mitigation funding, King County confirms that an entirely separate second advisory group will step in once operations begin.

DCHS currently runs neighborhood outreach through monthly virtual meetings, community events, and partnerships with local groups like Recovery Cafe, Peer Seattle, Lavender Rights Project, Capitol Hill Community Council, First Hill Improvement Association, East Precinct Advisory Council, and the GSBA. Once the facility opens, however, ongoing neighborhood relations will shift from the city-appointed SCAG to an operator-run panel.

“Connections Health Solutions, the operator for the future Seattle Crisis Care Center, will create a Community Advisory Council that reflects neighbors, the community and individuals with lived experience that they will regularly engage with once the center is open, similar to what is in place for the Kirkland Crisis Care Center,” the King County spokesperson said.

This overlap sets up two phases of community oversight. SCAG was created through city and county political channels to establish baseline CPTED design recommendations, shape operating agreements, and award one-time mitigation funds before the facility opens.

The upcoming Community Advisory Council will function as an ongoing liaison with the medical provider. It will handle day-to-day operational friction, community communication, and neighbor complaints once the building is open 24 hours a day.
The new, yet to be formed council will also have to live with the decisions being made today by the current advisory group including how the center’s Good Neighbor Policy operates in practice.

Connections Kirkland’s existing policy relies primarily on an email inbox and online web form for logging neighborhood complaints. There might be a need for something a little more robust when it comes to Broadway, Union, and Harvard Ave.

articles.title: No injuries after Saturday night apartment fire in 125-year-old building at 15th and Marion — UPDATE
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Seattle firefighters quickly extinguished a Saturday night blaze in a small 1901-era residential building at 15th and Marion just south of Madison.

Seattle Fire reports its crews were dispatched shortly before 9:00 PM following reports of a fire inside a multi-family residence. Seattle Fire Department described the structure as a two-story apartment building with a basement with the fire located on the top floor.
Firefighters got water on the flames, brought the fire under control, and initiated ventilation operations.

A search confirmed that all occupants had safely evacuated the building. Although smoke was observed issuing from the eaves, crews determined it was residual smoke from the second floor with no extension of the fire into the building’s attic space.
The structure has stood on the block for 125 years. Originally a single family residents, it was converted into a nine-unit apartment building and is today owned and operated by Cederstrand Rentals .
No injuries were reported. The cause of the fire was under investigation.
UPDATE : SFD tells us the fire was ruled accidental and “likely caused by ashes from incense falling onto a mattress and smoldering within the flammable materials.”
Fortunately, the damage was limited, with an estimated loss of only $1,000. Fire damage was limited to the mattress and floor underneath, the Seattle Fire spokesperson said.

articles.title: Clyde Hill Brokers Deal to Settle Growth Plan Complaint
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The tucked-away enclave of Clyde Hill is poised to create a new affordable housing incentive program, prompted by a legal challenge that city leaders have been attempting to settle for over a year. The modest tweak to its land use code, considered at a public hearing last week at the Clyde Hill planning commission, would grant property owners slightly more building rights in exchange for furthering the city's state-mandated affordable housing requirements.

Clyde Hill officials are set to sign onto this idea, slightly chipping away at the stringent zoning requirements that the city has touted for decades, in order to avoid a state growth board ruling that could potentially tear apart that armor even further. The adjustment illustrates the ways that relatively recent changes in state law continue to prompt even Washington's most exclusive jurisdictions to make moves to respond to a statewide housing shortage and affordability crisis.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Last April, the land use advocacy nonprofit Futurewise filed an appeal against Clyde Hill's newly adopted Comprehensive Plan, targeting shortcomings that mirrored those alleged in the group's appeal of the growth plan in nearby Mercer Island . The appeal asserted that Clyde Hill had failed "to document programs and actions needed to achieve housing availability including gaps in local funding," responding to a 2021 law that requires cities to plan for future residents across all income bands, among other requirements.
If Clyde Hill is able to reach a settlement, it will avoid having to defend its entire growth framework at a hearing at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board.

"We haven't had that hearing yet because shortly after the growth board challenge was brought by Futurewise, we entered into settlement discussions with them, and have been trying to create a compromise where maybe they don't get everything they're asking for in their petition," Clyde Hill City Attorney Jeff Taraday said Thursday. "But we change at least some of what they want us to change, and then as a result of that, we avoid having to actually have that hearing before the board, which is costly and, as with any litigation, fraught with some amount of uncertainty."

For a small city like Clyde Hill, with a median income of around $483,000 and virtually no land zoned for multifamily housing, the idea of "making adequate provisions" for households making a fraction of that amount has been a confounding one. Through 2044, the city has been required to plan for 10 new units of housing, a modest target in scale, but all of those units are aimed at households making less than 100% of broader King County's area median income (AMI), with three of those units targeted at households making less than 30% of AMI – approximately $40,000 for a family of two. Those type of units only get built with significant public subsidy.

Under the plan that was forwarded to the Clyde Hill Council by its Planning Commission Thursday, property owners who agree to build an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on their property that is rented to a household earning at or below 50% of King County's area median income for a period of 20 years would be able to increase structural lot coverage – the amount of space on a lot taken up by buildings – from the 30% cap currently in the code to 40%.

Alternatively, that 40% structural lot coverage could be achieved by paying a fee "in lieu" of building the unit, of a flat $400,000. Those funds would then be collected by the city and used to subsidize affordable units elsewhere, likely outside the city via A Regional Coalition for Housing (ARCH) .

The initial proposal, presented to the planning commission in August, also had additional building rights in the package, including a decreased rear-yard setback (from 35 feet to 20) and a decreased side-yard setback (from 15 feet to 10) on lots larger than 1,500 square feet. In addition, detached ADUs would have been allowed to rise to 25 feet tall compared to the current 12 feet. But those provisions ended up on the cutting room floor, in large part due to concerns over potential impacts on neighboring properties.

"I would rather live next door to a house that is a little bigger than I thought it was going to be than I would live next door to a house that is now five feet closer to me," commission chair Jared Wheeler said last month.
After scaling back the program to only include lot coverage, the proposal now appears to be viewed as the type of pill that Clyde Hill can swallow to get into compliance with state law.

"I sympathize with the concern about people's views being affected, but the state has mandated that we do more for affordable housing, this isn't our choice, and it appears that the majority of the burden is going to fall on the people who choose to either move here and build or build new houses," commissioner Spencer Hamlin said during Thursday's hearing.
Clyde Hill policymakers admitted they would like to mandate protection of views for homeowners, but that they realize state law likely precludes that approach.

"I think that the view encroachment is not good, but it's something that the people with existing houses are going to have to shoulder and bear, essentially, as part of them also accepting that this is the consequence of the state law," Hamlin said. "How do we spread out, fairly, all of the costs of this? I don't want my view encroached on either. Nobody does, but I don't see a reasonable scenario where you could do this and mandate protection of views. You'd have to blow up our building code."

So where did the $400,000 number, which one planning commissioner referred to a a developer's "golden ticket" to build a larger house on a lot in Clyde Hill, come from? Clyde Hill City Administrator Heather Thomas-Murphy said that it was developed in conjunction with ARCH, and is roughly tied to the cost to build one unit of affordable housing in the region.

"There's a lot of variables around the dollar amounts, but in general, they said $400,000 would be a justifiable number," Thomas-Murphy said. "The question is, what type of unit are we building, and where are we building it? It's more expensive to build in Clyde Hill than it is in some of our neighboring properties, but they said $400,000 was a good start."
A motion to lower the fee to $200,000 died at last week's meeting for lack of a second.
Thomas-Murphy told commissioners that Futurewise had indicated "conceptual support" for the proposal.

"With settlement discussions ongoing, we're limited in what we can say about the City's draft," Futurewise spokesperson Cat Huber told The Urbanist, instead pointing to the public ruling against Mercer Island from last summer. "Since HB 1220 , a city must identify land capacity for housing at each income level rather than in aggregate. Wherever a city counts on incentives or voluntary programs to produce that housing, the record must show how many units, at what income levels, or how much revenue those incentives can be expected to generate."

Futurewise sees its role as a "leading statewide public interest watchdog and legal steward of Washington's Growth Management Act" or GMA, which state lawmakers passed in 1990 to rein in suburban sprawl.

"Mercer Island's compliance filing, which is public, shows the kind of analysis that was put in that record," Huber continued. "That is the framework that applies to any jurisdiction's program, whatever form it takes. Futurewise continues to work collaboratively with Clyde Hill on solutions that meet GMA housing requirements and contribute to long-term community wellbeing."

Over its three plus decades of existence, the GMA has been relatively effective at limiting sprawl , but it's taken recent reforms to boost effectiveness at encouraging dense housing development within the urban growth boundary the law generated.

Clyde Hill is far from the only city getting nudged in this way. Futurewise is also negotiating a potential settlement with nearby Hunts Point, while the state's Department of Commerce remains in negotiations with Duvall after that city's Comprehensive Plan tried to sidestep many of these new requirements entirely. Meanwhile, the 2025 Housing Accountability Act created a new avenue of direct state review of housing growth plans, entirely outside of the Growth Management Hearings Board process.
The Clyde Hill City Council is expected to formally take up the affordable housing incentive program in November.

articles.title: What Will Become of the Empress Tree?
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: Taha Ebrahimi, professional tree nerd and author of Trees of Seattle: An Illustrated Walking Guide , sent a DM to our friend group chat on Wednesday morning.

“You guys!!! Vacilando is closing this Saturday!!!!! 😭😭😭😢” Ebrahimi included a link to Capitol Hill Blog’s story from the night before, which reported that the crumbling century-old building, which houses Bar Vacilando, Rione XIII, and Rubenstein Bagels, has been forced into vacancy due to ongoing structural and financial issues. The other shops closed immediately; Vacilando shuttered on Saturday, September 26.
My response, after “God fucking damn it,” was:

Bar Vacilando was lovely for many reasons, including its high ceilings, clean lines, herb-dusted fries with dippy garlic-curry aioli, and lightweight cherry tomato-infused martinis. But the jewel in its crown is doubtlessly the tiny patio’s 20-foot Paulownia tomentosa, aka the empress tree. The patio is conceptually inseparable from this sprawling and flamboyant tree, which grows from the brick foundation of the building next door, forming a leafy umbrella over the tables and blooming into a riot of fragrant purple trumpets in the spring. If you’ve never seen it, it has a sibling at the Seattle Japanese Garden in the Washington Park Arboretum. It’s like something out of a video game or an Ambien dream. To see it at its most splashy and ostentatious, one must visit an empress tree in late springtime.

So, when the bar goes, will the tree go? Ebrahimi said she had the same thought. A Stranger 2026 Genius Award nominee who’s been deemed Seattle’s Coolest Tree Expert , she estimates there are only about 30 empress trees in the city. “There’s one just a couple of blocks from [Vacilando], so part of me wonders if this one is a rogue tree that’s related.”

She adds that it’s one of the world’s fastest growing trees—growing up to 15 feet a year—and that in its native China, aristocratic families traditionally planted one when a baby girl was born so that it would mature alongside her and be ready to harvest when the family needed wood for a marriage dowry chest.

We began hatching a plan to try to save the empress, should the building face demolition. But where could it go? A container is a nonstarter—the empress tree grows so fast that it would become rootbound within weeks. It needs to live in the ground. Another issue: All signs point to empress trees not really tolerating their roots being disturbed. Its height and heft would be major obstacles to transplanting it as well. Maybe an arborist should be called? Could it survive a major pruning in order to bust it outta there? Carefully? If she can be moved, the empress tree at Vacilando ostensibly needs to live somewhere similar to a restaurant patio, where she grows from soil but drops her seeds over concrete.

To complicate matters, Washington state has had its little eyeball on this type of tree. The empress tree is really good at making more of itself, and it’s considered invasive in the Southwest and Eastern United States as such. Although it’s not officially considered a noxious weed here in Washington, it’s on the monitor list. Not a great situation for an imminently homeless tree.

Terrified that this beloved empress will be left behind to get crunched up along with the building, I fired off an email to Bar Vacilando’s parent company, Black Bottle Group, to ask what’s in the works here. Their response didn’t answer my question, except it actually did, without saying so.

“Thank you so much for coming to Vacilando over the years, and for caring about the beloved tree. When we took the space over 10 years ago, it was a single sprout issuing out of the brick, about two feet high. We’ve pruned it every year, it must have some water source, it has an incredible life force that has given us nourishment in every way that only Nature can. Thank you for your kind words. We are so grateful.”
Oh no. This is the Lynchian atmospheric whooshing of emails. Something bad is about to happen in this movie.

The next afternoon, I fled to the bar to ask questions in person. Stranger photo director and queer regenerative farm cofounder Billie Winter met me there. The tree looked bigger and more fabulous than ever, and we gazed up at its majesty. “The property owner is a ghost,” our very busy server said when asked what the fate of the tree might be, adding that it’s technically part of the building next door—currently home to Grandad’s Barber Shop—and not the one that housed Vacilando. “No one knows. Someone will probably take care of it, though!” Big not-my-problem energy. I would feel the same way if it were my second-to-last day of my job with maybe no notice.

Per Capitol Hill Blog, the barber shop building that the empress tree grows out of is not on the chopping block, just the one to the south. It’s easy to imagine the empress getting damaged in the process, of course. Both buildings are owned by somewhat-renowned local architect Gerald Kumata, who is 83 years old and seemingly not readily contactable. Perhaps a literal ghost as well. I thought back to the sage words of Taha Ebrahimi. “Get a photo of the source tree,” she’d texted earlier. “I’m certain it’s the source! It’s only two blocks to the east on 17th just north of Harrison! It had to have blown over to Vacilando.”

It was there. It was massive and fully mature, at least double the height of Vacilando’s tree. And it had TONS of seed pods. Most were cracked open and empty, but I jumped into the sky and managed to grab hold of a branch with more pods on it and pull it down. Billie had brought a little jar to collect the dusty, insect-wing-like seeds that remained in the walnut-like shells. In they went. I accidentally broke the branch, but it had a green shoot on there, which Ebrahimi said we could hypothetically propagate. “It will grow like gangbusters,” she wrote. “If you can cut a green shoot off, grow it in a vase until it grows roots!” I wrapped a wet paper towel around the base and stuck the whole thing in a Ziploc. A passerby asked if we were foraging for food, and we excitedly rambled at them about the empress tree at Bar Vacilando and how we’re pretty sure we found the mother tree. They wanted to follow @treeswithtaha on the socials and we told them how. At press time, we don’t have any real answers. Taha Ebrahimi is thrilled to hear that she was probably right and it was a rogue empress after all. Farmer Billie has a slew of seeds from the mother tree and, I’m sure, can germinate them easily. The green shoot is in a pickle jar of water in my kitchen window. I’m trying to figure out how to same-day-ship some root hormone to get it started. We can rebuild. Still, it’d be nice to save that poor patio empress. It seems crass to think that whomever is in charge of redeveloping and/or leveling the building in question would just destroy this elegant fashion icon without thinking. But I suppose we shouldn’t put it past some real estate developers, among the Disney-villainest characters in the land, to kill a pretty tree for being in the way. I accept that I am not in control of the fate of the Vacilando Empress, but look. If something bad is in the pipeline for her and someone hears about it, please let me know @megvanhuygen and I’ll figure it out. Hell, I’ll reconstruct Bar Vacilando’s patio in my backyard if I have to, frame by frame. Whatever needs to be done. This tree is loved by so very many. We’ll all make it happen.

articles.title: Campaign Finance Complaint Against Right-Wing Podcaster Brandi Kruse Dismissed
articles.author: John Stang
paras: Last week, the Washington Public Disclosure Commission, which regulates state political finances, dismissed a complaint against the conservative initiative group Let’s Go Washington (LGW) alleging the group received unreported in-kind political donations from right-wing podcaster Brandi Kruse.

LGW-sponsored initiatives on November’s ballot include measures banning transgender girls from girls sports , eliminating a new millionaires’ income tax, and to modify student privacy rights in schools. Kruse has publicly supported all three of these with extra emphasis on the trans girls sports ban.

The complaint filed by Washingtonians For Ethical Government (WFEG) alleged there were 157 instances of Kruse boosting the anti-trans measure on her podcast from September 2025 to February 2026, plus two times she led political rallies on the same topic. Almost daily on her podcast, Kruse criticizes trans girls participating in girls sports. The Washington Interscholastic Athletic Association says only 5 to10 such athletes compete statewide.

The PDC sent a letter to LGW stating it found no proof that the initiative group paid Kruse for her podcasted support of the trans girls measure. Even though one of Kruse’s daily advertisers is Future 42, a subsidiary of the political action committee Project 42 run by Let’s Go Washington co-founders Brian Heywood and Steve Gordon, the PDC found no proof they controlled the contents of her show, the letter said.
In 2024, Future 42 and Kruse said in interviews that the group and Kruse have an advertising relationship because of shared political views, but Future 42 doesn’t have any say in Kruse’s podcast.

LGW acknowledged it invited Kruse to help lead two political rallies for keeping trans girls out of sports, but also told the PDC that it didn’t sign any contracts with Kruse or make any payments to her. Kruse’s attorney Ashley Burman successfully argued to the PDC that rally participation and online commentary are not considered political donations under state law.

In a written statement, Heywood said WFEG spokeswoman Pam Stuart helped put together the complaint to distract from a LGW accusation that she allegedly harassed an LGW signature collector. “This complaint should have never seen the light of day, and we’re grateful the staff at the PDC can now return to matters that warrant their attention,” he said.

On a mini-podcast last week, Kruse said about the complaint: “The goal of this was never for it to be successful. The goal of it was to get months of negative headlines calling my integrity into question and to cast LGW in a bad light leading up to the election.”
Meanwhile, in a written statement, the WFEG argued its concerns about LGW and Kruse, who it called a paid internet influencer, are still valid.

“Washington voters have a right to know who is paying to influence their votes. The Public Disclosure Commission’s dismissal of our complaint against Let’s Go Washington leaves serious questions about that right unanswered in its letter declining to keep the matter open and investigate further. … Those unresolved questions deserve a closer look,” the WFEG’s statement said.
The WFEG claimed that Kruse provided at least $345,000 worth of in-kind donations with her podcast—an estimate that was never independently verified.

Kruse cannot decide whether she is a journalist or a political mouthpiece. Earlier this year, Kruse, right-wing activist Jonathan Choe, and conservative radio talk show host Ari Hoffman sued the state legislature’s Capitol Correspondents Association and the Washington House of Representatives Clerk’s Office for not allowing them press passes.

The association had been providing advice to the Washington House of Representatives Clerk’s Office when it reviewed press pass applications. But the House Democrats required clerk-approved press passes—approvals that the trio hadn’t been able to get because of their activity in partisan politics.

Due to the ban, the three filed a federal lawsuit against the House clerk’s office and the correspondents association to get approval to enter the Democrats’ side of the House chamber. That lawsuit is still ongoing, though US District Court Judge David Estudillo indicated after a March 10 hearing that they were unlikely to win.
Estudillo wrote that blurring the line between reporter and political activist would “raise questions about the motives of everyone in the press corps.”

Recently, the Capitol Correspondents Association signed an agreement with Kruse, Choe, Hoffman that said the correspondents association would not oppose the trio from getting press passes, wrote Jerry Cornfield, a statehouse reporter who’s also the association’s president, in an email to The Stranger .
With the Capitol Correspondents Association’s change of tune, the three plaintiffs dropped the association as a defendant in the lawsuit. The lawsuit is continuing against the House Clerk’s office.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, September 28–October 4
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Todd Hamm, Amanda Manitach, Charles Mudede, Langston Thomas, and Audrey Vann
paras: Show Me the Body, Whispers, Lip Critic, Truck Violence

(MUSIC) New York progressive punk trio Show Me the Body has always cut their art like a skater with a pen knife. Their early shows often took place under bridges, in basements, or on a whim if a kid on the internet invited them across state lines to do a flop-house show during a tour off-day. Their recorded material is equally raw collage work. Imagine heavily distorted punk played with banjo/bass/drums, spoken word ruminations surprisingly smoothly interlaced with hardcore tracks; imagine feeling fulfilled by the result. The trio has never compromised their cutting edge, even when introducing electronic elements or swapping in drummers; in fact, pushing the envelope has become a core tenet (see: Corpus I and II , their electro-punk/rap mashup duology). Their latest, Alone Together , contains all of the above and horns, breakbeats, and pigeons. ( El Corazon, 7 pm, all ages ) TODD HAMM
The Incredibly True Adventure of Two Girls in Love

(FILM) Director and screenwriter Maria Maggenti’s criminally underrated 1995 film The Incredibly True Adventure of Two Girls in Love should be required viewing for all sapphics (and everyone else, for that matter). When I first watched it, I wondered where it had been all my life, because it’s the sweet butchfemme teen romance and coming-of-age film of my dreams. If that isn’t gay enough for you, it also stars a young Laurel Holloman, aka Tina from The L Word , and Maggenti dedicated the film to her “first girlfriend … may our relationship finally rest in peace.” Holloman plays Randy, a young, hopelessly romantic masc high school student who works in a gas station and occasionally hooks up with an older married woman. When her popular, smart, wealthy classmate Evie stops by the station in her Range Rover one day, the two tumble into an innocent infatuation. The characters face realistic oppression and relationship struggles, but refreshingly, no one meets a tragic, untimely end, as is all too common with lesbian love stories. ( Northwest Film Forum, 7 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Tricky’s trip-hop classic Maxinquaye (1995) is a kind of ruins of the ’80s pop sound. Fragments of Trevor Horn are here, shards of Grace Jones are over there, and tremors of the Bomb Squad are felt everywhere—indeed, this is the “Aftermath.” One can also read Maxinquaye , which became associated with the Bristol Sound (Portishead, Massive Attack) as a kind of electronic mirror erected not towards the future but to the past, the last world. What we see by feeling this album, and also his masterpiece, Nearly God (1996), is that of the 20th century setting along the landscape of the ’80s. The song “Feed Me,” at the end of Maxinquaye , best expresses this essentially British dusk. Martina Topley-Bird, one of Tricky’s greatest discoveries, sings: “Feed me when I’m hungry drink me till I’m dry / The dream of yesterday becomes another lie / you feed me lies—distortion—the English disaster / no one is free from love for one master.” Tricky’s second album, Pre-Millennium Tension (1996) extended, to the point of utter darkness, the dusk in “Feed Me.” Tricky is a living legend. ( Neumos, 7 pm, all ages ) CHARLES MUDEDE

(VISUAL ART) Kelly Bjork’s work has always been about tenderness and the intimacy of interior spaces, but there’s another narrative threading through it: a personal reckoning. Their first solo show at J. Rinehart, Swimming Naked, marked the arrival of an imagery that was explicit, fleshy, and decidedly queer. In their new exhibition, Lunacy , that joyful, blissful raunch gives way to something darker, as Bjork dances with literal demons and confronts the spiritual, emotional, and physical disruptions of perimenopause. The work remains rife with impeccable patterns and intimate details sprinkled throughout like Easter eggs, but now those details reveal something grittier, wilder, and more brutally intimate than what’s come before. ( J. Rinehart Gallery ) AMANDA MANITACH

(MUSIC) Nick Hakim, the bard of the Outer Boroughs, has the voice of an angel, and most often, a vision to match. His songs, never in a rush to sensationalize his talents as a singer or guitarist, hit a sweet spot between Helado Negro, the often name-checked D’Angelo, and Bon Iver, and like those artists, his ear for slightly warped production and progressive song structures is where his soul shines through. Not everyone gets all gushy about the wispy tendrils of song Hakim provides, though—in fact, many a critic has accused him of staying too far in the pocket. “For godsakes, Nick, let your star shine!” they say. I will point you in the direction of a song called “Endlessly Waiting,” and let you decide for yourself. The track, from this summer’s I Can See , presents a haunting, dissonant piano line splashed upon itself, rolling on the ebb and flow of a hi-hat tick as Hakim’s aching lines are swallowed in a cave of reverb. If you also find yourself happily melting into each patiently stretched fiber of the song, I’ll see you there. ( Neumos, 8 pm, 21+ ) TODD HAMM
Styled by the Streets: Black Women in Hip-Hop Fashion

(FASHION/ART) When I think of the most important fashion moments in music, I think of Lil Kim’s purple pasty ensemble (and other iconic monochromatic looks), Missy Elliott’s inflatable trash bag suit, Salt-N-Pepa’s matching kufis paired with spandex bodysuits, and TLC’s fishnet tops that spell out their band name. Black female hip-hop artists take fashion risks when others won’t, and continue to innovate when other artists imitate (summed up by the Lil Kim lyric, “I used to wear Moschino, but every bitch got it / Now I rock colorful minks because my pockets stay knotted”). The Museum of Pop Culture’s newest exhibit celebrates this history, showcasing over thirty artifacts—that’s wigs, nails, clothing, and accessories—from across time, with pieces worn by icons like Mary J Blige, Lil Kim, Cardi B, and Doja Cat. ( Museum of Pop Culture, 10 am–5 pm ) AUDREY VANN

(FILM) The Filipino experience hardly fits within one set of borders. So it makes sense that the Diwa Filipino Film Festival also reflects this geographic boundlessness. Returning for its 12th edition, the Seattle-born, volunteer-run fest will screen a whopping 42 films telling stories from the Philippines and its global diaspora, spanning Bohol, Hiratsuka, Japan, and even 1940s Brooklyn. Across two packed days at the Wing Luke Museum, themed shorts programs explore migration, colonialism, generational trauma, activism, and that most universal of cinematic subjects: hopeless romance. Plus feature-length presentations bookend the fest, including the comedy No Room for Love , which follows artists weathering poverty and bad luck, and the closing-night film All the Things I Leave You (Patawid) , in which two young men uncover a decades-old love story. ( Wing Luke Museum, 10 am, 15+ ) LANGSTON THOMAS

articles.title: OPINION | Seattle, Make Arts and Culture Part of Our Year-Round Safety Strategy
paras: Dear Mayor Katie Wilson and members of the Seattle City Council,

We are artists, cultural workers, and stewards of creative and cultural communities and spaces who have dedicated our lives to the vitality of Seattle. We share your fundamental goal: a safe, thriving, and connected city. We are writing to you today to bring light to a tragically overlooked yet proven community-centered pathway to achieve that goal in the 2027–2028 budget.
This past summer, Seattle experienced something extraordinary: a historic decline in violence, including a celebrated " homicide-free June ."

We must look at the most significant and transformative change made in our city this year: the 2025 $3.6 million investment through the Office of Arts and Culture to activate our neighborhoods for the 2026 World Cup summer. Distributed to over 120 grantees, this funding generated more than 80 distinct public art and cultural activations all over the city from May to September of this year.

By paying local artists to bring life to our streets, parks, and business districts, the city fostered deep community engagement. These activations increased positive foot traffic, built relationships among neighbors, and created a vibrant cultural presence everywhere from north of downtown to the South End.

The link between community cultural investment and lower violence isn't just a Seattle story. A 2017 study of 264 U.S. cities indicates that community organizations have an important role to play in reducing violence and creating public safety. When cities support community solutions, homicide rates are shown to drop . This is consistent with other research that shows community engagement, environmental design, and creating positive spaces can decrease crime, as well as a study indicating that expanding library hours is correlated with a reduction in community violence.
This summer proved a critical reality: Art and cultural placemaking is public safety infrastructure.

This is not merely an exercise in Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED); it is also an active investment in healing. By resourcing existing creative networks, we are funding culturally relevant interventions that actively break cycles of violence. Artists and cultural workers are trusted messengers in their communities; when we fund their work, we are funding the social cohesion and collective care that true public safety requires.

Decades of research demonstrate that per capita officers do not reduce violence in communities. A meta-analysis that included 62 studies and 229 findings of police force size and crime found that per capita staffing did not reduce crime rates and that "this line of research has exhausted itself." A 40-year systemic review with meta-analysis of the efficacy of CCTV concludes " no significant effects observed for violent crime ."

Yet, the proposed 2027 budget misses a critical opportunity to build on the successes the city has had in violent crime reduction. Instead, amidst a $175 million deficit, the budget proposes a staggering $68 million increase to the Seattle Police Department to add 66 sworn officers and continues the mass surveillance that is putting vulnerable community members in greater danger.

We respectfully submit that such a massive expansion of the SPD budget is the wrong approach, particularly when the department is not suffering from a lack of resources, but rather from a bottleneck created by its own union's policies. As the inspector general's August 2026 report clearly outlined, the collective bargaining agreement negotiated with the Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG) actively throttles the efficacy of our Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department.

By contractually prohibiting CARE from responding solo to incidents on private property or those involving substance abuse and by granting SPD sergeants the power to veto CARE dispatches, SPOG has artificially manufactured an ongoing reliance on armed police for nonviolent crises.

We should not reward a system that deliberately limits our city's alternative crisis response capabilities with an additional $68 million. Throwing more money at a structurally constrained system is not a sustainable safety strategy.
We have a better model right in front of us. If we can fund community activation for FIFA and our summer tourists, we can — and must — do it for the people who call Seattle home year-round.
Therefore, we respectfully request that the City Council amend the 2027 budget with the following action:
Redirect $8 million from the proposed $68 million SPD budget increase into the Office of Arts and Culture (ARTS).
Dedicate these funds specifically for 2027 grantmaking in creative placemaking and public art activations.

This $8 million redirection is only a fraction of the proposed increase to the police budget, yet it allows us to more than double the 2025 investments in community-led public activations that brought us the first homicide-free June in Seattle since the 1970s.
By scaling up this highly successful "World Cup model," we can transform these 80 summer activations into year-round, comprehensive safety infrastructure across all Seattle neighborhoods.

This is not just arts funding; it is a direct investment in a proven public safety strategy. By beginning to value artists and cultural workers for the essential public safety infrastructure they provide, we can proactively build the healthy, vibrant, and safe neighborhoods that Seattle deserves without relying on constrained and overly expensive policing models.

articles.title: A First Look at the New Amtrak Cascades Fleet
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Train riders across the Pacific Northwest are just a few days away from a new era of regional train travel, with the first set of next-generation Airo trains poised to enter service this Wednesday . These shiny train cars and glistening locomotives will ultimately ply the rails on regional routes across the country, but the Amtrak Cascades routes from Vancouver, B.C. to Eugene, Oregon got first dibs, a fact that will bring real benefits on top of bragging rights.

On Saturday, the Washington Department of Transportation (WSDOT) and the Oregon Department of Transportation (ODOT) – which jointly operate the Cascades network – hosted dignitaries at King Street Station for a tour of one of the Airo trains and a ride south. Members of the public are also able to tour one of the trainsets on Sunday, but the free tickets to secure a spot for that tour in Seattle quickly ran out within half a day after their release last week.

The Airo trains, manufactured by Siemens, have been in development since 2021 , funded by the Biden-era Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. With 317 seats per train, these new models will give Amtrak Cascades a significant boost in passenger capacity, even if they will not initially enable any additional round trips or allow trains to travel significantly faster.

Though the Airo trains will be able to reach 125 mph on the Northeast Corridor when they go into service there late next year, they remain limited to 79 mph due to the existing rail infrastructure in the Pacific Northwest.

The passenger experience is significantly elevated on the Airos. The cars sport updated ergonomic seats featuring sturdy tray tables with device holders and USB ports – and a headrest-mounted reading light. Screens up and down the cabin cycle through providing destination information, locations for restrooms and the cafe car, and a seating chart that lets newly boarding passengers know which seats are already occupied.

Seat reservations are currently only available in cushy business class, but the trains include the infrastructure that would easily enable Amtrak to make the switch to seat assignments train-wide, ending the unneeded chaos of the Amtrak boarding line.

"The Airo is the cornerstone of Amtrak's broader effort to modernize trains, stations, and infrastructure across the country for a new era of passenger rail," Federal Railroad Administrator (FRA) David Fink said Saturday, illustrating the degree to which the Trump Administration also wants to be seen as a passenger rail champion. "We are building national momentum for future developments of these new sleek trains, beginning in the Northeast Region in late '27, and helping usher in a golden age of rail."

With three trainsets currently ready to roll, riders will be able to catch the Airo trains on the first trip of the day out of King Street in either direction. Train 503 heads south to Eugene at 7:10 am, returning to Seattle as Train 508 at 4:30 pm, while Train 516 starts its journey toward Vancouver, B.C. at 8:30 am and returns as Train 519 at 4:45 pm.

The third trainset currently on hand won't be used for passenger service right away and will stand by as a spare. Airo trains will replace older trains on additional Cascades runs as they complete testing through late winter, with three to four weeks between new each trainset going into service. All of eight of the trains are expected to be in Seattle by the end of the year, providing a big boost in overall capacity, particularly on the highly popular northern route to Vancouver.

The overhauled cafe car is sure to attract significant attention when the trains launch as well. The food items unique to Amtrak Cascades are still all available, including Alki bakery sandwiches and Ivar's clam chowder. While the booth seating right in the cafe is no longer in place, there are seats set aside in the rest of the cafe car for riders gathering to grab a bite.
The restrooms also got a significant upgrade, with automatic doors and touchless faucets and a selfie-friendly light around the mirror that activates when the door is locked.

Vertical bike racks will allow riders to bring their bikes directly on board with them, with 18 racks per train. Amtrak's online reservation system is still catching up with that additional capacity, officials said this weekend.

"Washington State has a rich history when it comes to rail travel," Governor Bob Ferguson said. "It's pretty central to who we are as a state and as a region, and throughout the Pacific Northwest. And that perhaps explains why rail travel is so popular here. The Amtrak Cascades corridor has over 1 million riders each year, and demand keeps growing, which is why this is such a huge, huge addition."

Continued improvements on the Cascades network will partly rest on Washington's shoulders. When Ferguson signed House Bill 1837 into law last year, the state committed to a goal of increasing on-time trip performance to 88% by 2035 (it was 61% last year), and ramping up the number of round trips to 14 between Seattle and Portland and five between Seattle and B.C.

That goal will be a tall order, given the state's limited control over BNSF railway, which controls most of the track mileage within the state, and the difficulty convincing legislators to sign onto incremental upgrades to rail infrastructure rather than flashy new projects.

While Amtrak has been showing off the Airo in cities up and down the I-5 corridor, Seattle will be their true home base. A new 100,000-square-foot maintenance facility , also funded by the 2021 infrastructure law, will provide space to be able to maintain these special trains, which have cars that can't be decoupled to perform maintenance work.

"The Airo trainset was developed for today's travelers with a focus on comfort, connectivity and convenience. This train is equipped with numerous accessibility features, such as onboard wheelchair lifts and accessible restrooms for passengers using mobility devices," Fink said. "And it will be a marked change from the Amtrak regionals, where the vestibules are wet when it rains or snowing when it's snowing outside. The trains are all connected together, so no more problems of leaking roofs or wet vestibules."

By next spring, when the Airo train is the only type of trainset ferrying riders up to Vancouver or down to Eugene, riders will likely start to take the new features for granted. But the Airo's arrival in the region is a major deal for rail travel, a signal that even if the trip is a little slower and less reliable than a flight... train riders still deserve nice things as well.

articles.title: Sunday Video: Seattle's Link Is Almost Too Good to Be Real
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Ray Delahanty of CityNerd did a video on the 2 Line, now that the light rail corridor spans Lake Washington connecting Seattle, Bellevue, and Redmond – and stretching north to Lynnwood in a segment overlapping with the 1 Line. Delahanty ranked the Eastside stations from worst to best. Toward the worse end of the spectrum was South Bellevue , which boasts a large parking garage, a u-pick blueberry farm and not a whole lot else.

Some lucky urbanists got to see an early version of the video along with commentary from our own Ryan Packer and two special guests who are leading transit policymakers (Claudia Balducci and Alexis Mercedes Rinck) at a Town Hall Seattle event earlier this month.

Both the video and the IRL talk also looked ahead to the next batch of light rail openings and explored the topic of Sound Transit 3 expansion plans, which are facing serious delays, especially in Ballard and Interbay . In typical CityNerd fashion, Ray eloquently summed up the dilemma with a dash of wry humor.

"I'm not naive; I understand how regional politics and bond measures work, but I don't think that makes it any less insane that Ballard has to wait 35 years longer to get light rail than a u-pick blueberry farm does," Delahanty said. "So being in Seattle in 2026 means being in a place where great optimism and great pessimism collide."

A big thanks to Ray for putting on the event with us, and for the kind words and member drive plug he shared at the talk and in the video. We are in the last days of our Fall Member Drive, and we could use your help to close out strong and hit our goal so we can keep growing The Urbanist.

articles.title: A rural Idaho county banned renewables. It’s having second thoughts.
articles.author: Julia Tilton, The Daily Yonder
paras: Jeff Hough did not pull any punches. What his fellow Republican county commissioners were about to do, he said to the packed courthouse, would violate America’s founding ideals. He quoted the Declaration of Independence to make his case.
The three-person commission was about to vote on an ordinance that would ban utility-scale solar and wind development in Bannock County, Idaho.
“We cannot deny the entire county the opportunity to exercise their property rights,” Hough said. “That goes against the principles this country was founded on.”
A few minutes after Hough’s emphatic speech , the ordinance passed by a 2–1 vote. Hough was the lone dissenter.

Since that consequential vote in March 2024, Hough has become the chair of the county commission and has dedicated himself to overturning that ordinance. He will soon have a chance to make that happen. This fall, Hough and the other two commissioners are set to vote on an ordinance with new language that would allow the development of solar and wind, along with nuclear energy, in the county.
The Bannock County vote is a test case of whether — and how — a community can revisit its assumptions about the costs and benefits of clean energy and decide to welcome development it once swore off.

In 2025, nearly 1 in 4 U.S. counties had some kind of ban, moratorium, or impediment to clean energy development, up from 15 percent of counties in 2023. More than 60 percent of counties with bans are rural, according to a Daily Yonder and Canary Media analysis of data from USA Today and the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University. (The Daily Yonder defines “rural” using criteria from the U.S. Office of Management and Budget .)

Bucking this national trend and reversing the ban would put Bannock County back in play at a moment when Idaho needs all the energy it can get. Idaho Power , the state’s largest utility, expects electricity demand to grow by 1 gigawatt by 2030, a roughly 26 percent leap from current levels.

“The need to build stuff now is critical to Idaho’s economic future,” said Aaron Menenberg, the Idaho policy manager for Renewable Northwest, a nonprofit working to decarbonize the region’s grid. “We can’t afford to say no to anything.”

Bannock County, nestled in a valley a few hours north of Salt Lake City and 100 miles west of Wyoming’s Teton Range, is a prime location for new power plants. It’s home to the Populus substation, a critical juncture for getting electrons onto the grid and into Idaho, Utah, Wyoming, and the Pacific Northwest. Building new power plants near a substation is cheaper, and those savings can help bring down costs for utility customers.

But the biggest opportunity for county residents, as Hough sees it, is not utility-bill savings: It’s economic development. In recent years, Bannock County’s population has grown far more slowly than Idaho’s. The county’s rural communities, meanwhile, are watching essential services disappear, and drought worsened by climate change is making it difficult for family farms to stay afloat.

Hough believes renewables would bring money into the community. Bannock County’s neighbors offer local proof: In 2024, projects in nearby Power and Bingham counties generated $909,000 and $639,000 in tax revenue, respectively. Hough wants to send a message — to the renewables industry and others — that Bannock County is “open for business,” too.

“Rural America is in a transition state,” Hough said from his office in Pocatello, the county seat, in July. “How do we make or help rural America … transition to this new way of life, so that they can thrive and prosper?”

Not everyone shares Hough’s vision of prosperity. In south Bannock County, Hough’s campaign has met with fierce opposition. Two camps exist: On one side are residents who are willing to lease their own land to solar energy developers or stand by their neighbors’ right to do so. On the other are those who are skeptical of renewables and believe that leasing land to developers is equivalent to selling out — many of them do, however, support nuclear.

Steve Criddle, a third-generation farmer and lifelong resident of south Bannock County, voiced his support for solar in 2024 before the ban passed. He described the situation today simply: “It’s confrontational.”
Bannock County’s moratorium on solar and wind stemmed from an unlikely source: Hough himself .
It was the fall of 2023, and he had just attended a conference of the Idaho Association of Counties in Boise.

At the conference, the Lava Ridge Wind Project , a 1-GW development slated for more than 57,000 acres of federal land in southern Idaho, dominated the conversation. County leaders from around the state were concerned about clean energy developers running roughshod over their communities. (President Donald Trump’s Interior Department canceled Lava Ridge in August 2025.)

The discussion got Hough thinking. Months before the conference, he had learned that several developers, including Chicago-based Hecate Energy and Moab, Utah–based Balanced Rock Power , were approaching landowners about solar projects in Bannock County.
When Hough returned from Boise, the cautionary tale of Lava Ridge fresh in his mind, he took action.
“I realized that we didn’t have any kind of ordinance,” Hough said. “So I knew they’d come in and do whatever they wanted.”

On October 12, 2023, spearheaded by Hough, the county commissioners voted unanimously to enact a six-month moratorium on large-scale energy projects. The idea was not to ban solar and wind, but simply to give the county time to regulate the developments and ensure they balanced economic opportunity with responsible land stewardship. A public hearing on the topic was set for the following February, and the commissioners would vote on the future of the moratorium in March.
But Hough’s moratorium took on a life of its own. In the months that followed, a group of concerned residents organized to make it permanent.

Rebecca Falcon led the charge. A decades-long resident of Downey, a town in south Bannock County, Falcon had been approached by Balanced Rock in September 2023 about leasing a portion of her 80 acres for solar. Appalled, she turned the company away. But Balanced Rock’s proposed Harmon Solar Project (aka Harmon I), a 300-megawatt solar facility with a 1,200-megawatt-hour on-site battery energy storage system, included her neighbors’ land. Stopping it would take more than just Falcon saying no.

Falcon and another neighbor, Dez Hauser, who had also turned away Balanced Rock, encouraged other concerned community members to show up to the February 2024 public hearing about the future of the moratorium.

By the time the hearing rolled around, residents had sorted themselves into two groups: for solar and against it. The meeting attracted such interest that it was moved from the county courthouse to a local high school auditorium in south Bannock County. The venue was still packed.
More than two dozen speakers, nearly all of them from south Bannock County, showed up to say their piece. The vast majority testified in opposition to solar.

The commissioners convened the next month to decide what to do with the moratorium. Hough voted to repeal it. The other two commissioners voted to extend it. The commissioners framed it as an additional pause to study the potential effects of large-scale renewable energy development in the county. Yet as the controversy mounted through the spring and summer of 2024, the county declined to take further action.
The ban stayed in place. Falcon, Hauser, and the other opponents had won.

Dale Lish, a grain farmer based in Downey, was frustrated with the decision. Recently retired from a career at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Lish became familiar with solar while working on projects in Idaho and Washington through the Rural Energy for America Program. He spoke in favor of the energy source at the same hearing where Falcon and Hauser expressed their concerns.

“The approach was just no to everything, which bothered me,” Lish said of the county’s decision, in a June interview on his property. “A straight-out ban — I don’t think that’s American. I think we, as private-property owners, ought to have a chance to do what we want within reason.”
In 2023, Lish signed a one-year contract with Hecate to option about 400 acres of his land for solar development. Hecate declined to renew the contract in 2024 because of the county’s ordinance.
The company has since pulled out of the county altogether. Representatives from Hecate did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

For the two and a half years since that March vote, Hough has been beating the drum of private-property rights while also trying to educate the community on Idaho’s power needs and how they might be met in Bannock County.

While the commission won’t vote until later this fall on the new ordinance, which is still undergoing public review, at least one of Hough’s colleagues may have changed his tune. Ernie Moser, an incumbent who supported the ban in 2024, said in an interview in June that his fears about solar and wind are “not as big” as they were two years ago. Still, Moser, who’s retiring from the commission at the end of this year, stressed that he wants “to do it right” when it comes to revisiting the county’s energy policy. The other commissioner, Ken Bullock, declined to comment.

May’s primary elections offered another indication of the county’s divided views. In the Republican primary, Hough faced a challenger from south Bannock County with an anti-solar platform, and though he won his race by 14 percentage points overall, his opponent captured 70 percent of the vote in Downey. No Democrat is running in the race, so Hough won’t face competition in the November general election.
This year’s results mirror those of 2024, when former county commissioner John Crowder, who voted for the ban in March of that year, won big in Downey but lost to Ken Bullock, an ally of Hough’s.
“In south Bannock County, it’s a supermajority of residents that do not want this,” Crowder said about solar development.

Steve Criddle can trace his family’s roots in Downey back to 1876, when his ancestors first filed paperwork for water rights. His grandfather farmed grain, including wheat. Criddle’s father did the same. He’s kept the agricultural heritage alive himself, but because of a changing climate, grain farming is no longer enough to sustain him.

“We don’t get enough moisture anymore,” Criddle said. The fields where he grows crops without irrigation now hardly produce enough to make ends meet. He’s turned some of his land over to cattle grazing and has worked odd jobs over the years to hold on to the farm.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Train Day!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: 2026 has been a big year for trains in Puget Sound. In January, the Federal Way Link Extension completed its first full month of operation. Simulated service on the 2 Line began in February , providing 4 minute frequencies for the first time between Seattle and Lynnwood. In March, the Crosslake Connection finally connected the 2 Line with Seattle. Link ridership jumped 46% in April thanks to the new service across Lake Washington. In May, the Sound Transit Board confirmed funding for several ST3 Link extensions (at the cost of other extensions). In June, Sound Transit welcomed passengers aboard new Sounder trains and set multiple Link ridership records . The USA vs Belgium World Cup match in early July helped Link surpass 300,000 passengers in one day for the first time ever. Last month, transit agencies in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties restructured their bus networks to cement Link as the backbone for regional transportation in Puget Sound.
To add to the list, Sound Transit is opening a new Link station and Amtrak is rolling out next-generation trains in September.

On September 30, Amtrak Cascades will welcome the first passengers aboard new Amtrak Airo trainsets. Amtrak Airo are trains built by Siemens that will soon run on many short distance Amtrak routes across the country. The first three of eight trains for the Cascades route are in Seattle and will operate on two roundtrips daily. The remaining five trainsets will enter service as they complete testing. An additional 75 Amtrak Airo trainsets will begin serving other routes around the country next year.

While the new trains will not reduce travel times or offer more daily trips, these trains can carry more passengers (over 300 seats per train), will be more reliable, and are more comfortable than the aging rolling stock currently used on Amtrak Cascades. Passengers can expect adjustable headrests, panoramic windows, enhanced lighting, and modern interiors.
Beginning September 30, Amtrak Airo trains will be used on the following Amtrak Cascades trips.
Between Seattle and Eugene: Train 503: Seattle to Eugene at 7:10am – 1:48pm Train 508: Eugene to Seattle at 4:30pm – 10:50pm
Between Seattle and Vancouver: Train 516: Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. at 8:30am – 12:30pm Train 519: Vancouver, B.C. to Seattle at 4:45pm – 9:10pm

Seattle Transit Blog will share a first look at the Amtrak Airo trains on Tuesday, including pictures and videos from a trip on the train. Until then, check out this Bluesky thread with highlights from the media tour on Saturday.

Also on September 30, Sound Transit will begin service at Pinehurst station. Pinehurst station is the agency’s first Link in-fill station and is located between Northgate and Shoreline South/148th stations. This the second piece of the ST3 measure to be completed (after Downtown Redmond Link) and will be the last Link station to open until Graham Street station in 2031. Pinehurst station is served by the new Metro Route 77 which connects the station with Bitter Lake and Lake City. 1 Line and 2 Line trains will begin stopping at Pinehurst station at 5am on September 30. The very first train to serve Pinehurst is a 2 Line train that departs Wilburton at 4:04am and arrives at Pinehurst at 5:05am.

To celebrate the new station, Sound Transit is hosting an event from 2pm-6pm on Wednesday. The event will include live music, local organizations, sponsors, food, an interactive activity with station artist Romson Bustillo, and the ST Shop merchandise booth.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
